transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-21
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~53 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Ethan Ross (Redwood SE), Lina Gomez (Ember Tech Head of Platform), Tom Wu (Cloud Engineer), Priya Nair (Security Lead)

Summary:
Quick discovery focused on Private/VPC deployment options for Ember Tech's internal LLM inference workloads. Primary topics: VPC peering vs PrivateLink, Private endpoints, region constraints (EU data residency and APAC), routing/NAT, KMS/HSM, SSO, and operational telemetry. Action items and next steps agreed.

Transcript:
[00:00:00] Maya (Redwood): hey everyone thanks for joining, uh we're Maya from Redwood, i'm the AE on this deal, and with me is Ethan our solutions engineer. we were sent your calendar invite, looks like lina tom priya, correct?
[00:00:12] Lina: yes hi thanks for making time, we're excited to learn more about private options, we run sensitive PII workloads and want to keep data in our AWS accounts if possible.
[00:00:25] Ethan (Redwood): great, can you give a quick overview of the current infra and what 'keep data in our AWS' means for you? VPCs, regions, compliance needs?
[00:00:38] Lina: sure. we have a primary prod VPC in us-east-1 and an EU cluster in eu-west-1. we also have a development account in ap-southeast-1 for APAC tests. main things: data residency for EU, SOC2 compliance, and we need strong audit logs. encryption at rest with our KMS is a must. we were thinking about VPC peering or PrivateLink to connect to a private Redwood endpoint.
[00:01:02] Ethan: ok. quick primer - Redwood Private can be deployed in a couple ways: we do a customer-managed private endpoint where our control plane is kept separate, or a fully private deployment that sits inside your VPCs. there are tradeoffs. for most enterprise customers we support VPC peering, AWS PrivateLink endpoints, or Transit Gateway attachments depending on scale and routing needs. peering is straightforward but is per-VPC; PrivateLink (interface endpoints) is more secure and doesn't require route table changes. TGW helps when you have many VPCs.
[00:01:36] Tom: peering is fine for a few VPCs, but we have multiple accounts and want minimal cross-account complexity. TGW might be better, curious about IP ranges, NAT and whether we need to open any public endpoints.
[00:01:50] Ethan: good question. for Private deployments we can avoid public internet entirely; we support interface endpoints and peering. transit gateway is recommended for many VPCs. regarding NAT, outbound egress for fetching updates or container images can be done through your NAT or through a tightly scoped egress path. we also support proxying updates through your network.
[00:02:12] Priya: what's the story for KMS and key management? we have a strict requirement for customer-managed keys, HSM-backed if possible.
[00:02:20] Maya: short answer, we integrate with customer KMS. for hosted cases we use our KMS but for Private deployments we can integrate with your customer-managed KMS; HSM-backed keys are something we can discuss as an enterprise add-on. i'll have ethan follow up with specifics.
[00:02:33] Ethan: yes we support AWS KMS CMKs. the runtime can be configured to use your KMS for encryption of customer data at rest. for HSM, typically customers use an HSM-backed KMS (AWS CloudHSM) and bring keys via KMS. we keep access minimal and audit all key usage in our logs.
[00:02:48] Lina: and audit logs - we need to ship logs into our splunk/elk stack, do you push logs to a customer S3 or do we pull?
[00:02:59] Ethan: we can do both. options: push audit logs to your S3 bucket in your account, or ship via a secure forwarder into your SIEM. for Private deployment we normally have audit logs stored in-customer or forwarded to your logging endpoints to satisfy compliance.
[00:03:15] Tom: region constraints - can the private runtime be deployed in eu-west-1? latency between our EU app tier and the inference layer is critical.
[00:03:24] Ethan: yes, we can provision Private in eu-west-1. in fact we recommend colocating inference with your app tier to reduce network latency. some model variants might only be available in certain regions initially; we'll share a region-capability matrix. also, keep in mind GPU availability per region - if you need specific GPUs that's a constraint.
[00:03:46] Lina: what's the difference between Redwood Dedicated and Redwood Private with VPC? we're evaluating both.
[00:03:53] Maya: Dedicated is reserved capacity that's still managed by Redwood but isolated logically - it's a dedicated pool in our infra. it's simpler to set up (no VPC peering) but data may transit our network depending on the deployment. Private is where the inference runtime is deployed inside your network boundaries (VPC) or via private endpoints so data never leaves your cloud account. Dedicated is good if you want predictable throughput without fully managing the network.
[00:04:18] Priya: ok, so for strict compliance Private seems required.
[00:04:22] Lina: yes for EU regulated data we'd prefer Private.
[00:04:25] Ethan: noted. another consideration is routing policies and failover. we can set up smart routing so EU requests stay in eu-west-1 and fall back to another region only if you permit it. failover is configurable per route.
[00:04:38] Tom: about private endpoints - are they interface endpoints (PrivateLink) or do you expose ENIs in our VPC?
[00:04:45] Ethan: for AWS it's typically interface endpoints (PrivateLink). under the hood those create ENIs in subnets you specify. we'll provide a CloudFormation/Terraform template to create the endpoints and security groups. we'll also provide sample route tables if peering is chosen instead.
[00:05:02] Lina: traffic egress - do calls to models make outbound calls to public model repos? how do we ensure model artifacts are pinned inside our network?
[00:05:11] Ethan: good point. we support model artifact mirroring into your S3 so the runtime pulls locally. if you want no public egress at all, we can coordinate mirroring and create an allowlist so runtime only talks to your S3 or private registry.
[00:05:26] Priya: and software updates/patching? we need a plan that doesn't open outbound holes.
[00:05:31] Maya: typically we have a scheduled maintenance window; for Private we can either push updates via your egress or allow your ops to pull signed artifacts from our s3 mirrors. we'll define the update patterns in the SOW.
[00:05:42] Tom: network ports - what needs to be open in security groups? we want to keep the attack surface tiny.
[00:05:47] Ethan: we'll give a minimal port list: TLS on 443 for endpoints, internal gRPC ports for node-to-node traffic can be limited to the VPC CIDR or specific subnets, and SSH only to bastion hosts if needed. the terraform has security group templates.
[00:06:02] Lina: does Redwood support SSO/SCIM for admin users and RBAC integration with our IdP?
[00:06:08] Maya: yes, SSO with SAML/OIDC and SCIM provisioning are supported. RBAC roles can be exported to integrate with your IAM and we can map groups to console roles. for Private we can also wire the control plane auth to your IdP if needed.
[00:06:22] Priya: any certifications we should call out? SOC2 is a must; ISO is nice to have.
[00:06:28] Maya: we have SOC2 Type II and are working toward ISO. i'll send the SOC2 report as part of the security packet.
[00:06:35] Ethan: and we also have pen test summaries and CNAPP findings; will include redacted reports.
[00:06:42] Lina: great. on the cost side - curious about unit economics: if we run private in our own account, what are the billing mechanics? do you bill for software only and we pay infra costs, or is it all through Redwood?
[00:06:55] Maya: with Private there are two common models: software-only licensing (you pay Redwood a subscription/usage fee and you own the AWS infra costs) or managed-private where we provision infra and include infra costs in a bundled price. most enterprise customers choose software-only when they want to keep infra on their bill for compliance.
[00:07:13] Tom: we prefer software-only so infra costs are on our side.
[00:07:16] Ethan: great. that also makes VPC peering and endpoint setup simpler from a billing perspective.
[00:07:21] Priya: logging retention - we need logs for 1 year; can you accommodate?
[00:07:26] Ethan: yes, logs can be forwarded to your S3 with lifecycle policies; retention is yours to enforce. we can also integrate with your SIEM for longer-term storage.
[00:07:36] Lina: one more networking question - do you support IPv6 inside endpoints? some of our infra is moving to dual-stack.
[00:07:44] Ethan: currently we support IPv4 for PrivateLink endpoints; IPv6 support is on the roadmap and we can give an ETA in the follow-up.
[00:07:52] Maya: ok sounds like priorities are clear: EU region deployment, KMS integration, SSO, audit logs, and a non-public egress model. next i'd like to propose concrete next steps.
[00:08:03] Maya: next steps proposed: we'll share the security packet and SOC2; ethan will prepare a network diagram and terraform snippets; lina/tom to share VPC CIDRs and primary AWS account ids. schedule a 30-45m SE deep dive next week.
[00:08:18] Lina: sounds good. quick question on performance - if we colocate in eu-west-1, what's expected latency? we use transformer-based models for real-time suggestions.
[00:08:28] Ethan: depends on model size and GPU type; for small-medium models in a colocated VPC you can expect single-digit to low double-digit ms per token in many cases. we'll run a small benchmark during the pilot to verify. also batching and KV cache can reduce cost/latency tradeoffs; we'll propose quantization options too.
[00:08:46] Tom: for the pilot, can we run a smoke test with a small model in our eu-west-1 account?
[00:08:51] Maya: yes that's typically how we start - pilot in your account with a small model, run benchmarks, then iterate. we'll put that in the SOW.
[00:08:59] Priya: legal questions - do you do DPA and data processing addendum? and can we have specific language for EU data residency?
[00:09:07] Maya: yes we have a standard DPA and can add data residency clauses; legal can follow up. we'll attach the DPA to the security packet.
[00:09:15] Lina: perfect.
[00:09:18] [background cross-talk - someone on customer side typing]
[00:09:25] Ethan: small note - for TGW we need permissions to accept attachments if we set that up; will include that in the setup doc.
[00:09:33] Tom: ok i'll coordinate with infra team about permissions.

[00:35:00] Maya: quick recap - i'll send security docs and SOC2, ethan will send terraform snippets and network diagram, and we'll schedule the SE deep dive for next week. customer to share VPC CIDRs and AWS account ids. agreed?
[00:35:14] Lina: agreed.
[00:35:20] Priya: agreed
[00:35:22] Tom: agreed.
[00:35:25] Maya: great thanks everyone. if anything else comes up email me directly. we'll aim to get the follow-up materials out in 48-72 hours.
[00:35:34] Lina: thanks, bye.
[00:35:36] Ethan: thanks all, bye.

[00:50:30] Maya: (wrap up) adding one more note - we'll include a short benchmark plan and suggested model sizes for the pilot, plus an estimate of GPU types per workload. you'll see that in the SE follow-up doc.
[00:50:48] Lina: excellent, appreciate it.
[00:50:52] Tom: thanks, talk soon.

Notes/links referenced during call:
